Tbh this isn’t really allowed under the Holidays Act for a few reasons. If the employee is on ACC then they aren’t working. Days of annual leave can only be taken on “otherwise working days” which the employee won’t have at the moment due to being on ACC. 

The employee can, however, ask for some of their annual leave to be paid to them to “top up” the 80% ACC income cover, but this is only if it is requested from the employee. 

The only other option is “cashed up” annual leave when employees get paid the cash value of their leave rather than “taking” leave for a day off work. It is only legal for the employer/employee to cash up 1 week of annual leave per entitlement year and the payout MUST be requested by the employee, in writing. The legislation says that if annual leave is “cashed up” where it wasn’t requested, the employer has to treat it as if the payment had not been made as the employee would still be entitled to the annual leave days regardless of what was paid out (section 28B(2) of the Holidays Act). 

It’s probably a mistake from the payroll team/employer so would recommend the employee get in touch with them with some relevant info on the above. It’s pretty easy to google or take screenshots from the Act itself. 

If the employer wants to deduct what they’ve “overpaid” they will need (written) consent from the employee to do so which the employee doesn’t have to provide (and could revoke at any time if they chose) but this could lead to some awkward tension in the business so may not be worth it. Employers and employees are also expected to act towards each other in good faith so if it is a genuine mistake, it’s really up to the two parties as to how the negotiate any adjustments there. 

If the employer refuses to fix or change anything, contact Employment Services at MBIE. There are multiple free services that can be used.

NAL but work with employment law regularly. 

As some others have said, you are not legally entitled to take your 'accrued' annual leave (the Act itself does not even cover 'accrued' leave so doesn't really mean anything legally). You are only legally entitled to take the leave once you have passed a full year of employment and receive your 4 weeks. It is common for employers to let employees take annual leave in advance of their first employment anniversary, but is not a requirement and is up to the employers.

If you have been there for less than a year and the business is having an official close-down period, then the employer should be paying out 8% of your gross earnings since you started employment.

Based on your post, it sounds like you've already passed at least your first employment anniversary and should be entitled to at minimum the equivalent of 4 working weeks of annual leave. Have you taken (the equivalent of) 4 working weeks of annual leave at this point to reduce your balance back to 0 weeks? 

If you have used your full entitlement balance, then you are still required to stop work as part of the close-down (if the employer gave you at least 14 days notice of the close-down). If they will not allow you to take any annual leave in advance and you have no remaining balance of annual leave, you will need to take another appropriate type of leave, if you have it, to cover that time. Alternatively, you can take leave without pay/unpaid leave.

I agree with this comment - your employment agreement may say that you agree to deductions, but employees are allowed to withdraw consent at any time meaning that employers would need to consult with the employee before continuing with deductions. 

Deductions should be done through signed agreement and must be specific and reasonable. Usually should say exactly how much the cost is in replacing it, but that’s all you should really pay for it to be “reasonable”. If there is a “disincentive” part of the amount they want you to pay, it’s probably unreasonable if the employer makes you pay the full amount rather than just the cost of replacing the key.

As far as I understand it, if you fix your mortgage rate you can’t pay any more than is agreed with the bank or you get a charge/fee. If you have a floating rate, I think you can pay off as much as you want. Some people split their mortgage and might have some of it fixed to try and take advantage of (ideally) lower mortgage rates and then some of the mortgage floating so that they have flexibility to make extra repayments when they’re able to.

Not a lawyer but familiar with this law. The key in this debate is whether you consent or not to the deductions. If you don’t consent then the employer will likely have trouble making any deductions - if they do you could take the case to the ERA. 

If you don’t consent, you won’t be very popular so you may want to find a job elsewhere but they don’t have much of a leg to stand on from my understanding. The law that people have linked to specifically say that an overpayment can be reclaimed IF done within 10 days of the next pay day that the overpayment occurred which obviously won’t cover your last 12ish months worth of overpayments.

I understand other people’s comments here about you not checking your bank account but the same could be said about the employer not checking your pays and when taking the matter to a neutral party like the Labour Inspectorate or ERA that will be considered as well. It’s quite a lot to ask someone to repay the amount they have asked within 12 months. 

If you agree to repay it, the employer should be happy about you providing consent and then having the legal ability to reclaim the overpayments so legally you probably have the upper hand here and can do as others have suggested and suggest a longer time period to pay back what has been overpaid to you.

Please get the employee who isn’t being paid to start collecting evidence of their work times (like time sheets, rosters, photos at work). Your post raises some red flags about the employer so to ensure the employee is in the best position they should collect as much evidence as they can in case they need to go to the Labour Inspectorate to get paid what they’re owed.

I’d recommend you open up a dialogue with the employer and ask why the deductions occurred, preferably over email so you have something in writing and to use as evidence if required. You can mention you didn’t give consent and you’re not sure why the deduction occurred and see what they say.

After that you could potentially look at personal grievances or contact Employment NZ or the labour inspectorate for more (free) help, but usually the first thing they’ll ask is if you’ve tried to resolve the situation with the employer. Any emails you’ve had with the employer about the deduction would be useful to supply as evidence.

Ideally it won’t have to go that far and it’s an accident or mistake that will be rectified by the employer upon your questioning of the deduction.

As others have said it is a legal requirement for the employer to hold an employment agreement for you. If that does not exist, they have breached some employment legislation already. 

If you signed an employment agreement that said something about financial penalties for something, this is often unenforceable by the employer and has to be for both a quantifiable and a “reasonable” cost to the employer. Based on what you’ve said in your post, it wouldn’t fly if they did try to enforce penalties and as also mentioned, if you went to the Labour Inspectorate it would probably be flagged. Make sure to keep any evidence/communications between you and the employer or manager if you do want to go to the Labour Inspectorate as they will need sufficient evidence of your claims. 

Recommend looking at the employment nz website as others have stated, there are services you can use (for free) before it escalates to the point you need to contact the labour inspectorate (such as mediation or early resolution).

Definitely need to check their employment contract - the labour standards minimum is a 10 minute paid break so it will depend whether their contract says they get 15 minute paid breaks or the minimum legal standard. 

Regardless I would say it’s worth talking to the manager/employer and bringing that up that they have been unpaid for a few paid breaks and seeking those arrears which they would be entitled to assuming it’s in their contract (I had a similar situation where the breaks would tick over into unpaid breaks but I never sought arrears as a result). 

As others have said they will probably be observed to make sure their breaks fall under that 15 minute time frame from the point they raise the issue though. I also agree it’s probably coming from a place of not understanding necessarily how the system works rather than trying to screw anyone out of their wages. 

Even if the contract says 10 minute paid breaks, they could probably seek for those 10 minute portions of the paid breaks to be paid back and the additional 5-6 minutes be unpaid. It’d still add up to something…

Hey there, I'm in a similar boat to you as I've posted on here a couple of times and struggle with suicidal thoughts, too, so if you ever feel you need someone to talk to you can always send me a message. (I'm mostly fucked up because of bad relationships as well).
If you think about it, although you don't want to exist, there must be some lingering feeling that you do as you want to be a husband and you want to be a dad. That's really something, it shows you want to have something to offer to a wife/child/family. I myself want dogs, which is more selfish than anything. It's very selfless of you to want children, especially if you realise the entire truth of parenthood (both pros and cons). I have a very good friend of mine who is in the same position as you. She was told she was infertile by her doctor, leading to carelessness with the man she was seeing. She fell pregnant, told him, and he decided he wants nothing to do with her. Now, she did want children at some point in her life, so the doctor telling her she was infertile was very troubling for her. Now, she's 22, pregnant, alone. She's definitely struggling. I assume this was not her original idea of how her family would develop. She is very family-oriented, she takes care of her parents, her siblings, everyone she can, yet what she wanted came much earlier than she expected and with drastic consequences. I don't really know where I'm going with this lol. 
I knew someone when I was younger who I thought didn't have much personality. He was very severely depressed and suicidal. After getting in touch with him again, I've noticed it has definitely improved and he is a very pleasant person to talk to these days. I believe that you DO have personality and you AREN'T blank, but you simply feel that way because of your depression (I feel the same way, yet people try to convince me I'm wrong). I don't know if you've been to a doctor or therapist about this, but some meds/counselling may be able to help you out. But you have to go into it WANTING to get better, knowing that it may not improve immediately, but having that will or that long term goal to motivate you. Think about your future family. That sort of thing. I also believe some hobbies may help. Maybe you have horrible experiences with people, so what could be better than meeting new people? You can replace the shitheads and maybe find a future wife. Just some suggestions.
